title: Frogs Swallow With Their Eyeballs (74% Harder Without) 🐸
description:
Why do frogs blink when they swallow? They're not blinking: frogs pull their eyeballs down into the roof of the mouth to push food toward the throat, and without that eye push a leopard frog needs about 74% more swallows per cricket.

Sources:
https://sicb.org/abstracts/contribution-of-eye-retraction-to-swallowing-performance-in-the-northern-leopard-frog-rana-pipiens/
https://www.discovermagazine.com/frogs-use-their-eyes-to-push-food-down-while-swallowing-1818
https://www.mentalfloss.com/animals/amphibians/frogs-eat-their-eyes-literally

topic: Why do frogs blink when they swallow?
script:
Frogs actually swallow with their eyeballs.
You've just never noticed why.
Watch a frog gulp down a cricket,
and its eyes squeeze shut
and sink right into its head.
That's not a blink.
A frog's eye sockets are open underneath,
with no solid bone floor.
So muscles yank each eyeball down,
into the roof of its mouth.
Now those eyes press on the bug like two thumbs,
shoving it back toward the throat.
Why bother?
Frogs don't chew.
Their tiny teeth only grip,
so dinner goes down whole.
Scientists tested this on leopard frogs.
With those eye muscles switched off,
each cricket took 74 percent more swallows.
About four gulps instead of two.
So a frog's eyes spot the bug,
then help push it down.
Next time a frog blinks at you,
is it winking,
or eating?
key_facts: Most frogs retract and close their eyes repeatedly while swallowing (Levine, Monroy & Brainerd, northern leopard frog study, 2004)
Retractor bulbi muscles pull the eyes down into the mouth, where they press on the prey and push it toward the throat
With those muscles denervated, swallows per cricket rose 74%, from about 2.3 to 4.0
Frogs swallow prey whole; their small teeth only hold it
